card.hook: Plot twist: the Bodleian isn't one building, it's a group of five, and the round dome everyone photographs is just one of them. Good news is the best view of it is a short walk from the High Street.
card.stand_here: Stand on the steps of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin, on the south side of Radcliffe Square. Face the Radcliffe Camera, so Brasenose College is on your right and the Old Schools Quadrangle sits behind the dome.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the dome, Brasenose College and the Old Schools Quadrangle all fit. Try 2x (or higher, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the stonework. Use 0.5x only if you want the whole square, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome slightly off-centre with Brasenose College as the right-hand edge, then tap the dome and go a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, which really helps in the square and in Brasenose Lane. Soft daylight is lovely on the stone.
card.selfie_here: Try the Wren door in the outdoor Old Schools Quadrangle. One venue guide calls it a picturesque photo spot, so it should make a nice backdrop. Use the front camera, stand close to the door and check what's behind you before you tap.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you with a Bodleian building behind you, stand in front of the Weston Library entrance on Broad Street and ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the street, facing the library front so the building fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are fine, but selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the Bodleian buildings. No photos in the Radcliffe Camera or in old reading rooms like Duke Humfrey's Library.
card.challenge: Get the dome with Brasenose College as its right-hand edge, then walk to Brasenose Lane and catch the Camera peeking out at the end.
card.good_to_know: The Bodleian was founded in 1602 by Sir Thomas Bodley and is one of the oldest libraries in Europe. The Radcliffe Camera dates from the 18th century, and Duke Humfrey's Library was completed in 1488. The church tower gives a view down over the Camera, but it may cost a fee, so check the official site first.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the steps of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin, on the south side of Radcliffe Square. Face the Radcliffe Camera, so Brasenose College is on your right and the Old Schools Quadrangle sits behind the dome.

card.hook: Turn around on the pavement on St Aldate's and there it is: Tom Tower, sitting dead centre above the college gate like someone drew it with a ruler. It's one of the most balanced pictures in Oxford.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement on St Aldate's, directly opposite the Tom Gate entrance, and face east across the road to the gate and the tower above it. Stay on the pavement, because buses use this road.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole gate and tower. If people or parked vehicles stop you stepping back, try 0.5x. Use 2x when you want to get closer to the upper part of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the arch on the centre line so the two wings balance left and right, and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the day for fewer people on the pavement. If you're still around in the evening, try night mode with your phone braced against a wall or post. Great Tom, the tower's bell, rings 101 times at 9:05 pm.
card.selfie_here: Walk into Christ Church Meadow from St Aldate's and look on your left for Christ Church Memorial Gardens. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and put the college and its flower beds over your shoulder. Tom Tower should show up on the left of the view. The riverbank inside the Meadow also works, facing back toward the college, with open grass behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement directly opposite the Tom Gate entrance, so your full height and the tower, arch and wings all fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: St Aldate's is a busy road with buses, so cross with care and stay on the pavement while you frame your shot. You can photograph the gate and tower from the public pavement without a ticket, but going inside the college needs one, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the picture with the arch on the centre line and nobody wandering through the gateway. People walk through all the time, so take a few frames and see if you can catch it empty.
card.good_to_know: Henry VIII founded Christ Church in 1546. Its chapel is also Oxford's cathedral, which is unusual. Tom Tower was designed by Sir Christopher Wren, and behind the gate is Tom Quad, the largest quadrangle in Oxford.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement on St Aldate's, directly opposite the Tom Gate entrance, and face east across the road to the gate and the tower above it. Stay on the pavement, because buses use this road.

card.hook: Tall columns, a wide flight of steps and a stone front so neat it practically poses for you. This is one of the easiest buildings in Oxford to photograph, even if you only have a minute.
card.stand_here: Stand on Beaumont Street, in the heart of Oxford, and face the museum's columned front. Cross to the other side of the street and step back a little if you want the whole front in one shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full front. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x, but it can bend the edges of the building. For the columns and carved details, go to 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a flat line so the building doesn't lean, then tap the front of the building and slide darker if the sky is washing out the stone.
card.best_time: Soft, even light on an overcast day, or in the morning or late afternoon, makes the stone look its best. Go at a quieter time if you want a clear view of the steps.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little higher than your face. Turn so the columns sit over your shoulder and check that the roofline looks level before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the pavement on the Randolph Hotel side of Beaumont Street, out of the road and clear of the entrances, while you pose in front of the museum.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep clear of the road and the entrances while you take photos. Inside, the museum asks visitors not to use selfie sticks or flash, and photos aren't allowed where an object label shows a private loan or copyright restriction. Check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Get one wide shot where a person on the steps makes the columns look huge.
card.good_to_know: The building you see today dates from 1841 to 1845 and was designed by Charles Cockerell. The museum is Britain's first public museum. Its first home was on Broad Street, which opened in 1683 to house the collection Elias Ashmole gave to the University of Oxford. The Taylor Institution on the corner with St Giles' is part of the same building and uses the same Ionic style.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Beaumont Street, in the heart of Oxford, and face the museum's columned front. Cross to the other side of the street and step back a little if you want the whole front in one shot.

card.hook: Walk down Brasenose Lane and the big stone dome slides into view at the end of the narrow lane, like a curtain going up. It's the best bit of theatre in Oxford, and it's free.
card.stand_here: Stand in Radcliffe Square, out on the open cobbles. The Camera is about 26 m to the east of it, only a few steps away, so face the dome.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole dome and drum in from close up. Step back and switch to 1x, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome's details and the tower behind it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the drum up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive. The square gets busy from mid-morning.
card.selfie_here: Try the Catte Street corner beside the All Souls College side of the square, where the corners frame the Camera and the colleges. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the dome over your shoulder, and check the framing on the spot, because it can be tricky to fit yourself in without losing the view.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand just outside the entrance of The Vaults & Garden cafe, opposite the Camera, and shoot straight on while you stand on the cobbles with the dome behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Camera is not open to the public, and photography isn't allowed inside, so this is a spot for exterior photos only.
card.challenge: Take the same shot three times: from the square, from Catte Street and from Brasenose Lane. Then pick a winner and tell your friends it was obvious all along.
card.good_to_know: The Radcliffe Camera was designed by James Gibbs and built between 1737 and 1749. It was paid for from the estate of the physician John Radcliffe, who left £40,000 when he died in 1714. Today it is a reading room for the Bodleian Library.

card.hook: Here's an honest take: the Oxford Union is a good street-level photo, not a big sweeping view. That suits it, because the Gothic brick and stonework sit right above the pavement, and the street line walks your eye straight in.
card.stand_here: Stand on St Michael's Street, on the north pavement, and face the south side where the Union's main block stands. The Venetian Gothic front and its 1910 extension rise above the street in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the front of the building with the street around it. If the pavement is narrow and you can't fit the full height in, tap 0.5x, then try 2x for the details in the brick and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, holding your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, so you can see the detail in the brick and stone. Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the street, which helps when you're waiting for a gap in the passers-by.
card.selfie_here: Try the Cornmarket end of Frewin Court, where the debating hall is visible. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x and tilt up a little, so the hall sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the St Michael's Street pavement facing the Union frontage, where the 1910 extension can be glimpsed, and stand with the building behind you; check the shot, as the whole building may not fit.
card.rules_and_safety: The Union is a private members' society, so take your pictures from the public street and keep clear of doorways. The Frewin Court gate isn't a public entrance and the Cornmarket-side gate is locked, reached only from New Inn Hall Street, so check access first.
card.challenge: Can you get a shot where the street line leads right to the building, with nobody walking through the middle? Patience wins.
card.good_to_know: The Oxford Union is a debating society founded in 1823. Benjamin Woodward designed its first buildings, which opened in 1857, and Alfred Waterhouse's debating chamber followed in 1878, then the largest purpose-built debating chamber in the world. The original chamber became the library, which now holds over 60,000 volumes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on St Michael's Street, on the north pavement, and face the south side where the Union's main block stands. The Venetian Gothic front and its 1910 extension rise above the street in front of you.

card.hook: Picture 11 metres of carved Haida totem pole rising through a room packed with glass cases, with a mezzanine on each side looking down. That's the Pitt Rivers, and it's a bit of a showstopper.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, in the main colonnaded room, where you can see the floor, the cases and the upper levels. Then turn to face the totem pole.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the tall room, the upper levels and the totem pole. Switch to 1x for single display cases, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for small objects and labels, so you don't have to lean on the glass.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a bright object in a case, then drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the lit cases don't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the room is quieter, so you can step back and get clear views. Opening times vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the arched wooden door of the Pitt Rivers, inside the Oxford University Museum of Natural History. From the dinosaur skeletons, turn left at the Darwin statue and it's in the corner. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the arched door over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed for personal use, but flash and selfie sticks are not. Check the museum's official site for its current photography rules before you visit.
card.challenge: Find a case full of the same kind of object, then take one neat pattern shot of the repeated rows, with no reflection of you in the glass.
card.good_to_know: The museum was founded in 1884 by Augustus Pitt Rivers, and the building was finished in 1886. It started with about 22,000 items and now holds more than 600,000. Objects are grouped by how they were used, not by age or origin, which is why you see so many versions of one tool side by side.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, in the main colonnaded room, where you can see the floor, the cases and the upper levels. Then turn to face the totem pole.

card.hook: Picture a cathedral spire that wandered into town and got stuck in the middle of a bus junction. That's the Martyrs' Memorial, and it's a lot more fun to photograph than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of St Giles' and Beaumont Street, at the south end of St Giles' where Magdalen Street also meets. The memorial rises a little to the south-east of you, so face that way to get the Cranmer statue looking back at you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole spire and the street around it into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the statues and carved detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter, with fewer people and less traffic in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Use the junction where St Giles', Magdalen Street and Beaumont Street meet, with the Ashmolean side behind you. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tuck the spire over your shoulder. People also gather around the stepped base, but keep your feet on the ground.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on St Giles' a short way north of the memorial, facing south, while you stand on the pavement by the junction with the memorial behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Climbing on the monument isn't allowed, so enjoy it from pavement level. The memorial sits on a busy traffic island by the main bus route, so take care crossing and wait for gaps in the traffic.
card.challenge: Can you get the pointed tip of the spire, one of the three statues and a passing bus all in one frame without the spire leaning?
card.good_to_know: The monument remembers Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, three Protestant churchmen executed in the 1550s. George Gilbert Scott designed it, modelling it on the medieval Eleanor crosses, and it was finished in 1843. If you're walking on, the actual execution site is close by in Broad Street, marked by an iron cross sunk into the road.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of St Giles' and Beaumont Street, at the south end of St Giles' where Magdalen Street also meets. The memorial rises a little to the south-east of you, so face that way to get the Cranmer statue looking back at you.

card.hook: Broad Street does half your work for you: the whole street leads your eye straight to the Sheldonian, which has been posing for photos since it was finished in 1669.
card.stand_here: Stand on Broad Street, outside Trinity College, and look east with the theatre on your right. You should see the Sheldonian's facade with the Clarendon Building beyond it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic street view. If the pavement is busy and you can't step back far enough, switch to 0.5x to fit it all in, then try 2x for the carved details and the cupola.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building edges up with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight suits the pale stone. If the sky is bright, tap the stonework and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the stone keeps its detail.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement outside the perimeter railings on Broad Street, by the railings with the stone Emperor Heads, with the theatre behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and let the theatre sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at ground level on the cobbles on Broad Street in front of the entrance railings and face the theatre, so the whole facade fits in the frame while you pose.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography for personal use is generally allowed inside, but check for restrictions, and photos are generally not allowed during events. The steps up to the cupola are steep and narrow, and the theatre can close for ceremonies and concerts, so check the official site for access before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the street empty and one with a cyclist whizzing through, then pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: Christopher Wren designed the Sheldonian for the University, and it was built between 1664 and 1669. It's named after Gilbert Sheldon, who paid for almost all of it. It was built for degree ceremonies and still hosts ceremonies, concerts and lectures, with room for up to 700 people. Look for the D-shaped plan and the eight-sided cupola. It's Grade I listed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Broad Street, outside Trinity College, and look east with the theatre on your right. You should see the Sheldonian's facade with the Clarendon Building beyond it.

card.hook: Imagine a church for science, with a glass roof held up by slim iron pillars and stone columns that are each cut from a different British stone. That's the court inside the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, and it's a gift for your phone.
card.stand_here: Head to Parks Road, where the phone icon on the map sits at the middle of the museum building. Once you're inside the great square court, stand where you can see the full width of the glass roof, with the pillars lined up on each side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole glass-roofed court and the long arcades. Switch to 1x for statues and arches, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for carved leaves, column tops and details high on the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the pillars up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, then tap a bright part of the roof and slide it darker so the glass doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the glass roof lets in the most light. A quieter moment makes it easier to get the court without people in the way.
card.selfie_here: Head out to the front lawn on Parks Road and stand beside the huge dinosaur footprint with the museum building behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so more of the building squeezes in, and tilt the phone up a touch.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Museum Road, far enough back to fit the whole neo-Gothic façade in the frame, while you pose in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: Indoor photos for personal use are reported to be fine, but skip the flash, and check the museum's official site for its photography rules before you start shooting.
card.challenge: Find one carved leaf or branch on a column or the ironwork and fill the whole frame with it. Bonus points if you can tell your friends which stone it's sitting on.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1860 and was designed mostly by Benjamin Woodward with Thomas Newenham Deane. It hosted the well-known 1860 evolution debate, and it's Grade I listed, as is the neighbouring Pitt Rivers Museum. Much of the decoration was never finished because the money ran out, and the displays are being renewed in phases until July 2026, so some cases may look different from older photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Parks Road, where the phone icon on the map sits at the middle of the museum building. Once you're inside the great square court, stand where you can see the full width of the glass roof, with the pillars lined up on each side.

card.hook: Picture a punt gliding along the Cherwell, a wall of green trees behind it and Magdalen College's tower poking up above. That's the postcard shot, and you get it without paying to go inside.
card.stand_here: Stand on Magdalen Bridge at the south end and look back across the Cherwell. The garden's riverside edge is to the west, with the tower rising behind the trees.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the garden edge, the river and the tower in one frame. Want the tower to feel closer? Try 2x. Use 0.5x only if you need more river, and keep straight lines away from the edges so they don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the river in the lower third, with the trees and tower above it.
card.best_time: We don't have a set best time for this view. Early morning or late afternoon is worth a try, since the light is softer and the bridge may be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Inside the garden, try the arched doorway in the stone wall. Hold your phone at arm's length with the front camera and let the arch frame you for a secret-garden look. The wildflower meadow area also works: face the front camera with the flowers and planting behind you. Switch to 0.5x if you want more garden over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge and Christ Church Meadow are public land, but the walled garden and glasshouses are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a punt to drift into the lower part of your frame, then take a few shots in a row and keep the best one.
card.good_to_know: Oxford Botanic Garden is the oldest botanic garden in Great Britain. It was founded in 1621 as a physic garden for growing medicinal plants. It packs more than 5,000 plant species into about 1.8 hectares. Its front entrance, the Danby Gate, was designed by Nicholas Stone in 1632-33 and is Grade I listed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Magdalen Bridge at the south end and look back across the Cherwell. The garden's riverside edge is to the west, with the tower rising behind the trees.

card.hook: You come in for a quick look and end up nose to nose with a cheese counter, a flower stall and a hand-painted sign, all within about ten steps. The Covered Market is a photo scavenger hunt with snacks.
card.stand_here: Stand right on the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the market. Turn on the spot until you find the lane with the best depth, then face down it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch a whole lane stretching away. Switch to 1x for shop fronts and stalls, then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for signs and produce, so you don't have to lean over the counters.
card.make_it_pop: Tap on the brightest part of your subject, then nudge the brightness down a touch so the shop lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day tends to be calmer, so you can get the lanes without crowds. Daylight from the entrances helps a bit too.
card.selfie_here: Stand beneath the hanging Alice characters with the high roof behind you, and hold your front camera at 0.5x to fit it all in. If the Y.O.U shop front is still showing its decorated selfie panel, that's another fun backdrop, and it asks you to tag the shop. Either could have been changed or moved, so treat them as a bonus.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before taking close photos of traders or customers, and don't block the walkways. Opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a hand-painted sign, then get it in the frame with a lane stretching away behind it.
card.good_to_know: The market officially opened on 1 November 1774, to move untidy stalls off the main streets. John Gwynn, who also designed Magdalen Bridge, drew up the plans and designed the High Street front with its four entrances. It's been Grade II listed since 2000, and around half of the traders sell food, including butchers making the Oxford sausage.

card.hook: Oxford has a lane so narrow that the walls do half your composing for you. Walk in, look up, and there's the Bridge of Sighs floating over your head.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Catte Street and New College Lane, at the Catte Street end of the lane, and face east along it. Keep the bridge in the middle and let the lane walls frame both sides.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the bridge with the lane walls around it. Try 2x if your phone has it, to bring the bridge closer without moving. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of wall and roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines to line the bridge up in the centre, tap the bridge, and if the sky at the far end looks washed out, slide it a little darker.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet for a calmer lane and a better chance of an empty frame. If it's busy, wait for a gap or snap a few shots in a row.
card.selfie_here: Stand on New College Lane directly under the bridge arch, where the lane runs beneath the span. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and keep the bridge above your head.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand further back in the lane at the Catte Street end, facing east, while you stand closer to the bridge so they can frame you with the lane walls and Hertford College's upper floors.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is private Hertford College property and visitors can't cross it, so stay in New College Lane. The lane and the outside of the bridge are public and free to photograph.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the walls perfectly symmetrical, then walk round to Queen's Lane and find the bridge again with the Bodleian Library walls behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Bridge of Sighs crosses New College Lane in central Oxford. It belongs to Hertford College, and you can see the college's upper windows beyond it. Visitors can't walk across, but the view from the street is free at any time.

card.hook: Most people photograph a castle head-on and wonder why it looks flat. Here, you let a little stream lead your eye to a chunky stone tower instead.
card.stand_here: Stand on Quaking Bridge, looking north or southeast across the Castle Mill Stream. Face whichever way brings St George's Tower into frame, with the water in front and the tower rising behind. From the bridge it's about 2 minutes on foot to the castle.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the stream, the tower and a bit of sky together. Tap 2x to fill the frame with the tower. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of water, because the tower will look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, then leave the bottom third for the stream.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework, and early on weekdays the bridge is likely to be quieter. If it's busy, Pacey's Bridge is a calmer spot for another stretch of the same stream.
card.selfie_here: Try the riverside path beside the Castle Mill Stream, between St Thomas' Street and Park End Street. Face away from the tower, use the front camera at 0.5x, and let the tower and the water sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Quaking Bridge and shoot north up the water while you stand on the stream path below the castle walls.
card.rules_and_safety: The castle's interior, prison and tower climb are ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go. If you do climb the tower, take all your tower photos while you're up there, because visitors can't go back up unsupervised.
card.challenge: Get the tower perfectly upright on a gridline with the water in the bottom third, and bonus points for a walker passing by to show how big it is.
card.good_to_know: Oxford Castle was begun in the early 1070s by the Norman baron Robert D'Oyly the elder, who used a branch of the Thames to help form a moat. St George's Tower is now thought to be a Saxon watch tower from around 1020 that the castle later absorbed. The site later became the county prison, which closed in 1996 and is now a hotel and visitor attraction.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Quaking Bridge, looking north or southeast across the Castle Mill Stream. Face whichever way brings St George's Tower into frame, with the water in front and the tower rising behind. From the bridge it's about 2 minutes on foot to the castle.

card.hook: Picture a long stone bridge, trees leaning over the water and a row of punts bobbing below it, all in one frame. That's Magdalen Bridge, and it's the kind of view that makes you stop mid-stroll and reach for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand inside Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum, by the river. From here the bridge lies to the east, so face across the Cherwell with Magdalen College behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the bridge, river and punts in together. If your phone has zoom 2x, try it to pick out the arches and the college without the foreground crowding in. Use zoom 0.5x only if you're close to the water and want the trees and punts in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the line of arches along the top third and let the water fill the rest, then tap the bridge and drag the slider a touch darker so the sky and stonework keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon are best, when the sun lights up the bridge. The garden view works all year, but entry is charged and opening hours vary, so check the official site first.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the Magdalen Bridge historical marker, where Cowley Place meets The Plain, so the bridge is directly behind you (the Victoria Fountain is on the traffic island nearby). Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze more in, and check the bridge is in the frame before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a fellow visitor inside the Botanic Garden to take your photo, with you by the river and the bridge across the water behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge carries traffic as well as pedestrians, so keep well clear of the road. It's also closed on the morning of 1 May for the May Morning crowds. Angel & Greyhound Meadow, a riverside alternative, often floods, so check conditions locally.
card.challenge: Can you get a punt or an overhanging branch tucked into one corner of your shot, so the bridge feels like it has a bit of depth?
card.good_to_know: The present bridge was built between 1772 and 1790 and has 11 arches of different sizes. It replaced a much older medieval stone bridge, and the first known mention of a bridge at this crossing dates from 1004. It was widened on the south side in 1882 to take a tramway, but the original design was kept.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand inside Oxford Botanic Garden and Arboretum, by the river. From here the bridge lies to the east, so face across the Cherwell with Magdalen College behind it.

card.hook: Most people hurry past St Mary's porch on the High Street. Stop and look: the columns are twisted like barley sugar, and a Virgin and Child sit in a shell-shaped niche above them.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the University Church of St Mary the Virgin on the north side of the High Street, and face the church. Step back a little along the High Street frontage to fit the porch and spire together.
card.zoom: Zoom 0.5x from close range gets the porch and the base of the tower in. Zoom 1x gives a straighter, more natural view of the frontage, and zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the carvings, the statues and the top of the spire.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the gridlines on and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, and keep your phone level, tilting it up only a little.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in your shot. Check how the light falls on the porch, since the frontage faces the High Street.
card.selfie_here: Head into Radcliffe Square and stand on the south side, between the church and the Radcliffe Camera, with the church behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze the spire in over your shoulder, and check which way you're facing before you snap.
card.ask_someone: Stand in Radcliffe Square and ask a passer-by to photograph you with the church in frame and All Souls College on the left of the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't permitted during services, as this is an active place of worship. The tower is reached only by a narrow 127-step medieval turret staircase with some steep, worn steps and no lift, and access may change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the Virgin and Child in their shell-shaped niche, then get one shot of the tower standing dead straight against a grid line.
card.good_to_know: The porch dates from 1637 and was designed by Nicholas Stone. The spire went up in the 1320s, and of its twelve statues only one is original; the rest were put up around 1894. University meetings were held here from at least 1252, and in 1555 the church hosted the trial of the Oxford Martyrs.

card.hook: Four busy streets meet at Carfax, and in the middle of the bustle stands one lonely stone tower, like it's waiting for a bus. That's your photo: the tower with all of Oxford swirling around it.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, right by Carfax Tower on the north-west corner of the crossroads. Then step back across the junction until the whole tower fits, and face it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower plus some street. Switch to 1x for a more natural look. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the clock face and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines, and keep your phone upright so the tower doesn't lean. If the sky is bright, tap it and slide a touch darker so it keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early in the day tends to be calmer around the crossroads. Soft morning or late-afternoon light is also kind to the stone.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold your phone a little low and out in front of you. Turn so the tower rises over your shoulder, then check that the top isn't cut off.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand across Queen Street from the tower and face it, while you stand near the tower, so they can fit the whole thing in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch the traffic and the pavement crowds when you step back to frame your shot, and keep to the pavements. If you plan to climb the tower, the staircase is narrow, steep and spiral, and one review says it's not suitable for very small children or people with mobility problems. Check the official site for current opening times.
card.challenge: Get the clock face sharp and the street life around the tower in one shot, then sneak a close-up of the old tombstone behind it.
card.good_to_know: The tower is all that remains of St Martin's Church, which dates back to the 12th century and was the city's own church for centuries. It stands about 23 metres (74 feet) tall, and the city council says no building in central Oxford should be taller. The clock chimes the quarter hours, and six bells ring out on special occasions.

card.hook: Picture a Longhorn cow chewing away in the long grass while a cathedral spire pokes up behind the trees. That's Christ Church Meadow, and you're standing right in the middle of Oxford.
card.stand_here: Stand on Broad Walk, near the St Aldate's entrance, and face east across the meadow. The grass fills the bottom of your shot and the college towers and cathedral spire rise behind the trees.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the meadow and skyline. Try 0.5x for more sky and grass, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the towers and spire closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper third line and let the grass fill the lower part of the frame, with the spire just off-centre.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, because the gates are locked at night. In winter the meadow can flood, so paths may be wet or closed.
card.selfie_here: Try Christ Church Memorial Gardens, on the left just inside the gate as you enter from St Aldate's. Use the front camera, go to 0.5x and hold the phone a little low, so the college shows above the garden and greenery behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: If cows are in view, keep a respectful distance and use zoom rather than walking closer. Drones are generally not permitted here, and the gates are locked at night.
card.challenge: Get a cow in your foreground with the spire behind it, and don't take a single step closer to do it.
card.good_to_know: James Sadler made the first balloon ascent by an Englishman from this meadow on 4 October 1784, and a plaque records it. Rowing events like Eights Week and Torpids are held on the Thames beside it. The meadow is owned by Christ Church but open to the public during the day.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Broad Walk, near the St Aldate's entrance, and face east across the meadow. The grass fills the bottom of your shot and the college towers and cathedral spire rise behind the trees.

card.hook: Picture a big square tower rising over the river, with punts drifting lazily underneath. Magdalen (say "MAWD-lin") does this all day, and it's very good at it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Magdalen Bridge. The main college buildings and the tower are about 194 m to the north-west, so face that way with the river in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the tower, river and punts in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer without stepping into the road. Use 0.5x only if you want the whole bridge, because the tower will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line, leaving a bit of river at the bottom so the tower has something to rise from.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and the light is softer than at midday. Avoid 1 May (May Morning), when the bridge is very crowded for the dawn gathering and good angles can get blocked.
card.selfie_here: One Oxford photo guide picks the Magdalen College Cloisters as a favourite, because the tower shows in the background. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the tower rising behind your shoulder. Check the angle when you get there, as it's only described as having the tower in the background.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Magdalen Bridge over the Cherwell and ask your helper to frame you with Magdalen Tower in view beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower isn't open to the public, so you'll be shooting from outside. Access to the college grounds may be limited, so check the official site first. On the bridge, stay on the pavement and watch the traffic.
card.challenge: Take one frame with a punt drifting past and one with the river empty, then pick your winner.
card.good_to_know: Magdalen College was founded in 1458 by William Waynflete, Bishop of Winchester. Since the days of Henry VII, the college choir has sung from the top of the tower at 6 a.m. on May Morning. Inside the grounds there's a deer park and Addison's Walk.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Magdalen Bridge. The main college buildings and the tower are about 194 m to the north-west, so face that way with the river in front of you.

card.hook: Most old streets make you squeeze into a doorway to fit anything in. Broad Street, or "The Broad" if you want to sound local, is wide enough that you can step back and get whole rows of old frontages in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Clarendon Building steps, at the north-western corner, and keep to the pavement rather than the road. Face along the street so the historic facades frame your shot, with the Clarendon Building's arch and the Sheldonian Theatre in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full width of the street and all those facades. Pop back to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details like the Sheldonian's stone heads or the Clarendon Building's arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the street up with the lower third of the frame, so the buildings rise on both sides.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be the quietest. Degree ceremonies at the Sheldonian bring crowds and gowns on many dates, which adds atmosphere but makes a clear view harder.
card.selfie_here: Head to the carved stone heads around the Sheldonian Theatre's railings, which look out across Broad Street. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the heads and the street sit behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from the north-western corner of the Clarendon Building steps, or from the opposite side of the road (on the pavement) if groups fill it.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't stand in the road for the picture: motorists and cyclists aren't very forgiving of tourists, and the 20mph limit is often ignored. The colleges may close to visitors at short notice, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few shots and pick the one where no cyclist photobombs your facade. Bonus points if the stone heads are in it too.
card.good_to_know: Broad Street was once called Horsemonger Street because it was Oxford's horse market. The Clarendon Building (1711-15) was designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor, and the Sheldonian Theatre (1664-68) by Christopher Wren. The Old Ashmolean, built in 1683, was the world's first museum to open to the public, and a cross of granite setts in the road opposite Balliol marks where the Oxford Martyrs were burnt in the 16th century.

card.hook: New College is one of Oxford's oldest colleges, and most of it hides behind high walls. So the street front on Holywell Street is the shot, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Stand on Holywell Street, opposite the Robinson Tower entrance, and face south towards the college. Keep the gateway right in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a calm, natural view of the tower and gateway. If the whole street front won't fit, tap 0.5x. For tower details, try zoom 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the tower with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go when the street is quiet if you want fewer people in your frame. If the sky is bright, tap the tower stonework and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its detail and the stone doesn't wash out.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Holywell Street pavement across from the Robinson Tower entrance gate, with the tower behind you. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a touch so the tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Holywell Street pavement while you stand in front of the tower's gate, so the whole tower fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The college grounds aren't open public land, so check the official site before you plan to go inside. Photography is not generally allowed in the Great Hall or Chapel.
card.challenge: Can you get the tower perfectly straight on the gridlines, with the gateway dead centre and the long stone front running off to both sides?
card.good_to_know: William of Wykeham, Bishop of Winchester, founded New College in 1379, and it was the first Oxford college designed around a main quadrangle. The long Victorian front you're photographing is called 'New Buildings' and was built between 1872 and 1896. George Gilbert Scott designed part of it, and Basil Champneys did the rest, including the Robinson Tower over the gates.
